concept.title: Infinite Color Wheels: No Nontrivial Neighbor‑Blend Colorings
concept.concept_description: We conjecture that the finite Chromonic Lemma extends to infinite, locally finite, strongly connected digraphs. Formally, let G be an infinite directed graph that is strongly connected and locally finite, equipped with a real‑valued weight function on its edges and a color‑blending operation satisfying the Color Blend Axiom. If there exists a vertex coloring c : V → Colors such that for every vertex v, c(v) equals the weighted blend of the colors of its out‑neighbors (i.e., c(v) = π_{(u,p)∈Out(v)} p·c(u) ), then c must be constant. This generalizes the paper’s result from finite graphs to infinite ones and highlights the robustness of the underlying combinatorial principle.

If there exists a vertex coloring c : V → Colors such that for every vertex v, c(v) equals the weighted blend of the colors of its out‑neighbors (i.e., c(v) = π_{(u,p)∈Out(v)} p·c(u) ), then c must be constant. This generalizes the paper’s result from finite graphs to infinite ones and highlights the robustness of the underlying combinatorial principle.
concept.lean_guess: Extend the finite proof via a compactness/ultraproduct construction: take an increasing sequence of finite subgraphs exhausting G, apply the finite Chromonic Lemma to obtain constant colorings on each subgraph, then use an ultralimit to build a global coloring satisfying the neighbor‑blend condition. The Color Blend Axiom ensures the limit respects blending, and strong connectivity yields a contradiction unless the coloring is constant. Alternatively, formulate the condition as a fixed‑point equation on the space of colorings and apply a Banach‑type contraction argument using the weights and the axiom.

concept.title: The Mathematics of Deja Vu: Fixed Points in Consciousness and Cognition
concept.concept_description: Deja vu — the feeling that you've experienced something before — is a fixed point in a dynamical system. Model cognitive state as a function f: S -> S mapping current brain state to next brain state. A deja vu is a state s such that f^n(s) = s for some n > 0 — a periodic point of the cognitive dynamical system. Conjecture: By Sharkovsky's theorem, the existence of a period-3 orbit in the cognitive dynamics (three distinct states that cycle) implies chaos in the sense of Li-Yorke, meaning there exist uncountably many cognitive trajectories that are neither periodic nor convergent. Moreover, the set of deja vu states (periodic points of f) is dense in the cognitive state space S if f is continuous and S is an interval. The frequency of deja vu (occurring in ~70% of people) corresponds to the natural density of periodic points in a typical chaotic map. Test: model cognitive dynamics as a logistic map f(x) = rx(1-x) on [0,1] with parameter r chosen to match empirical deja vu frequencies. For r = 3.83 (period-3 window), compute the density of periodic points and compare to the 70% lifetime incidence. Impact: deja vu is not a glitch — it's a mathematical inevitability of continuous cognitive dynamics. Any continuous cognitive map with a period-3 orbit MUST have deja vu.
